title: Areithous the Mace-man
greek: κορυνήτης (korynētēs), 'club-man', from κορύνη (korynē), 'club'
short: An Arcadian hero famous for fighting with an iron club instead of bow or spear; Nestor later tells how Lycurgus killed him by guile in a narrow pass.
body: Areithous carried the unique title korynētēs, 'club-bearer' (LSJ), because, as Nestor explains at 7.138-41, he broke enemy ranks with an iron mace rather than with bow or long spear. Lycurgus (an Arcadian, not the Thracian king of Book 6) caught him in a pass too narrow to swing the club, speared him and stripped the armour Ares had given him; in old age Lycurgus passed it to his squire Ereuthalion, whom the young Nestor killed (7.142-56). Pausanias was shown the 'narrow way' and a tomb of Areithous in Arcadia (8.11.4) and lists Lycurgus among the early Arcadian kings (8.4.10); Leaf thinks the local tradition grew out of the epic rather than the reverse. Leaf also notes a chronological knot: the Areithous of 7.8-10 lives at Arne in Boeotia and has a son fighting at Troy, which fits Nestor's story only if two men bore the name. Iron weapons are rare in Homer, where bronze is normal, so the iron club marks Areithous as exceptional.

title: Helenus the seer reads the gods' plan
greek: σύνθετο θυμῷ βουλήν (syntheto thymōi boulēn)
short: Priam's son Helenus, a prophet, perceives the plan Athena and Apollo have just agreed and prompts Hector to issue a challenge to single combat.
body: Helenus was introduced in Book 6 as the best of the Trojan bird-diviners (6.76). Here he 'understood in his heart' (thymōi) the gods' plan: Leaf stresses that this means by prophetic insight, not by overhearing. Aristarchus athetized 7.53, where Helenus says he has heard 'the voice of the gods', on the ground that a seer knows such things by his mantic art; Leaf calls the objection frivolous, since prophets habitually describe revelation as a voice. Leaf finds the previous line, 'not yet is it thy fate to die', more open to objection, because nothing in the gods' talk supports it and Hector's later words (7.77) and his fear before Ajax (7.215-16) hardly suggest he believed it. The scene is a typical case of double motivation: the gods decide, and a human intermediary turns their decision into human action.

title: Athena and Apollo as vultures
greek: ὄρνισιν ἐοικότες αἰγυπιοῖσι (ornisin eoikotes aigypioisi)
short: Athena and Apollo perch on Zeus's oak in the form of vultures to watch the duel; Homer's gods often appear as, or like, birds.
body: Leaf argues that the poet means the gods actually take the shape of birds: eoikotes here is 'in the likeness of', not merely 'after the manner of'. Comparable transformations include Athena as a swallow on the roof-beam at Od. 22.240 and Sleep perched in a fir tree like a bird at Il. 14.289-91. Some interpreters preferred the weaker sense to spare the gods' dignity; Leaf replies that gods sitting in human form at the top of a tall tree would be no more dignified. The aigypios is a large bird of prey; Leaf notes that the name seems to cover both eagles and vultures, since the aigypios also takes live birds (17.460). The oak is presumably the one near the Scaean Gate where the two gods met (7.22, 7.60). The picture of divine spectators 'rejoicing in the warriors' turns the duel into a spectacle staged for the gods.

title: Simile: the ripple of the West Wind
greek: Ζεφύροιο ... πόντον ἔπι φρίξ (Zephyroio ... ponton epi phrix)
short: The seated armies, bristling with shields, helmets and spears, are compared to the dark ripple a newly risen west wind spreads over the sea.
body: The noun phrix means a 'shudder' or ruffling of a smooth surface, the ripple a gust drives across calm water (LSJ). It picks up the participle pephrikuiai, 'bristling', used of the ranks just before (7.62), so the comparison turns on a single root: the ranks 'shudder' with weapons as the sea 'shudders' under the breeze. Leaf takes the point of comparison to be the glint of armour above the seated men, like light on the ripple; the darkening of the sea beneath the wind (7.64) adds the massed colour of the troops. The same word describes the black ripple from which Proteus rises at Od. 4.402. The simile catches a moment of eerie stillness between the formal challenge and the fighting, as both armies sit to listen.

anchor: Our oaths the son of Cronos
title: The broken oaths of Books 3-4
greek: ὅρκια μὲν Κρονίδης ὑψίζυγος οὐκ ἐτέλεσσεν (horkia men Kronidēs hypsizygos ouk etelessen)
short: Hector's brief, almost offhand reference to the solemn truce of Book 3, which the Trojan Pandarus broke in Book 4; he blames Zeus rather than Troy.
body: In Book 3 both armies swore oaths that a duel between Paris and Menelaus would decide the war; in Book 4 Pandarus' arrow broke the truce. Hector now says that Zeus 'brought not the oaths to fulfilment', a striking evasion of Trojan guilt. Leaf (Introduction to Book 7) thought 7.69-72 an interpolation designed to join two originally independent duel stories: a second duel on the same day, undertaken without apology for the broken truce, seemed to him close to anticlimax, and he found support in the manuscripts' reading at 7.73, which runs on naturally if the four lines are absent. Whatever their origin, the poet keeps the breach in view later in the book: Antenor admits that the Trojans now fight 'after proving false to our oaths of faith' (7.351-2), and the theme of perjury hangs over Troy's fate.

anchor: my body let him give back
title: Return of the body for burial
greek: σῶμα δὲ οἴκαδ᾽ ἐμὸν δόμεναι πάλιν (sōma de oikad' emon domenai palin)
short: Hector's terms: the victor may strip the loser's armour but must give back the body for burial, the very treatment Akhilleus will later refuse him.
body: Stripping a fallen enemy's armour was the victor's right and the proof of his success; withholding the body from burial was the extreme of dishonour. Hector proposes that the loser's body be returned so that his people may give him his 'due meed of fire' (pyros lelachōsi), that is, cremation. Leaf notes that 7.79-80 recur almost word for word at 22.342-3, where the dying Hector begs Akhilleus for exactly this and is refused. The conventional chivalry Hector offers here therefore carries heavy irony for anyone who knows the poem's end, where his own body is ransomed only by Priam's journey in Book 24. Hector also promises to hang the captured armour on Apollo's temple at Troy (7.82-3), a dedication of spoils to the god who gives him glory.

anchor: heap up for him a barrow
title: The burial mound (sēma)
greek: σῆμά τέ οἱ χεύωσιν (sēma te hoi cheuōsin); ταρχύσωσι (tarchysōsi), 'give burial'
short: The heaped earth mound on the Hellespont shore is the Homeric grave-marker, a 'sign' (sēma) that keeps a warrior's name alive for passing sailors.
body: Hector imagines the Greeks 'giving burial' (tarchyein) and heaping a mound by the Hellespont. tarchyō is a solemn word for funeral rites; Leaf, following Helbig, connected it with taricheuō, 'to preserve, embalm', and suspected a memory of embalming in honey, but LSJ judges that connection improbable, so the etymology remains disputed. Leaf also observes that the many ancient grave-mounds visible along the Hellespont shore probably suggested the speech. The word sēma means literally 'sign': in the Odyssey the shade of Agamemnon tells Akhilleus that his tomb was raised on a headland by the broad Hellespont so as to be seen far out at sea (Od. 24.80-4). The Homeric rite is cremation followed by a mound, as in the funerals of Patroclus (23.245-57) and Hector (24.785-804).

title: Kleos: fame that does not die
greek: τὸ δ᾽ ἐμὸν κλέος οὔ ποτ᾽ ὀλεῖται (to d' emon kleos ou pot' oleitai)
short: Kleos, literally 'what is heard', is the fame that outlives a hero; Hector imagines it carried by a future sailor who reads a tomb.
body: kleos comes from the verb klyō, 'to hear' (LSJ: 'rumour, report', then 'fame'): glory is what other people say about you. Hector's speech is a miniature theory of epic. A stranger 'of men that are yet to be' sails past, sees the mound and speaks two lines that read like an epitaph, naming the dead man only as Hector's victim. The irony is double: the fame Hector imagines is his own, won by killing another man, and the tomb that preserves it belongs to that man. The closing half-line is a formula: Odysseus uses it of Zeus' portent at Aulis, 'whose fame shall never perish' (2.325), and Akhilleus later speaks of the 'unwithering fame' (kleos aphthiton) he will win if he stays at Troy (9.413). Leaf compares the device of the imagined future speaker at 6.459-62, where Hector imagines someone pointing to Andromache as a slave.

anchor: shame had they to deny him
title: Aidōs: shame against fear
greek: αἴδεσθεν μὲν ἀνήνασθαι, δεῖσαν δ᾽ ὑποδέχθαι (aidesthen men anēnasthai, deisan d' hypodechthai)
short: Shame (aidōs) pulls the Greek chiefs towards accepting Hector's challenge, fear pulls them back: a perfectly balanced line on the heroic dilemma.
body: aidōs is the sense of shame or respect felt before the judgment of others (LSJ: 'reverence, awe, respect for the feeling or opinion of others... shame, self-respect, sense of honour'). Refusing the challenge would be shameful in the eyes of both armies; accepting it means facing Hector. The verse sets the two verbs against each other, 'they felt shame to refuse, they feared to accept', and the long silence follows. Aidōs is the social glue of the warrior class throughout the Iliad: leaders rally the army with the cry 'Shame, Argives!' (aidōs, Argeioi, 5.787, repeated by Agamemnon at 8.228), and Hector refuses to retreat at 22.105 because he feels aidōs before the Trojans and their wives (as already at 6.442). In Book 7 the paralysis is broken by Menelaus' outburst, Nestor's taunt and finally the lot, which shares out the risk without dishonour.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed.), s.v. αἰδώς (reverence, awe; shame, self-respect, sense of honour)

title: Menelaus' curse: 'turn to earth and water'
greek: ὑμεῖς μὲν πάντες ὕδωρ καὶ γαῖα γένοισθε (hymeis men pantes hydōr kai gaia genoisthe)
short: Menelaus curses his silent comrades to dissolve back into the stuff mortals are made of: earth and water.
body: Leaf paraphrases the curse as 'may you rot away to the elements of which you were made'. The belief that human beings were moulded from earth and water is old and widespread: in Hesiod's Works and Days Zeus orders Hephaestus to mix earth with water to make Pandora (WD 60-1), and the scholia quote the philosopher Xenophanes, 'for we are all born from earth and water' (fr. B33 DK). Menelaus opens by quoting Thersites, 'women of Achaea, men no more' (2.235); Leaf finds the speech's harsh tone at odds with the courteous regret elsewhere typical of Menelaus. It also explains his rash decision to arm himself, which Agamemnon at once restrains. Menelaus closes, however, with a pious reflection that 'the issues of victory are held by the immortal gods' (7.101-2).

title: 'Even Achilles shudders to meet him'
greek: καὶ δ᾽ Ἀχιλεὺς ... ἔρριγ᾽ ἀντιβολῆσαι (kai d' Achileus ... errig' antibolēsai)
short: Agamemnon claims that even Akhilleus dreads meeting Hector: a rhetorical exaggeration to stop his brother, contradicted elsewhere in the poem.
body: Leaf notes that there is no incident in the Iliad to which this can refer, and that it contradicts Akhilleus' own claim at 9.352-5 that while he fought Hector would not venture beyond the Scaean Gate and the oak. It is best read as rhetoric for the moment: Agamemnon, protecting his brother, inflates the danger. An ancient critic quoted in the A scholia thought 'he is far better than thou' rude to Menelaus and wished Homer had said 'he is the mightiest of all'. The remark also keeps the absent Akhilleus before the audience. Leaf points out that his absence is what emboldens Hector to challenge and makes the Greeks hesitate, and Ajax will say as much when he faces Hector (7.226-32).

title: Nestor's appeal to old Peleus
greek: γέρων ἱππηλάτα Πηλεύς, ἐσθλὸς Μυρμιδόνων βουληφόρος ἠδ᾽ ἀγορητής (gerōn hippēlata Pēleus, esthlos Myrmidonōn boulēphoros ēd' agorētēs)
short: Nestor shames the chiefs by imagining the grief of Akhilleus' father Peleus, who once questioned him eagerly about every Greek family.
body: Nestor's rebuke works by invoking an absent elder whose judgment the younger men must fear. He recalls a visit to Peleus in Phthia, told more fully at 11.765-90, when Nestor and Odysseus came to recruit Akhilleus and Patroclus for the war. Peleus is 'driver of chariots', 'counsellor' and 'orator of the Myrmidons'; the unspoken irony is that his own son is sitting out the fight. Leaf notes that Herodotus (7.159) makes a Spartan envoy adapt this very line, substituting Agamemnon for Peleus, which suggests it had become proverbial (though Leaf allows that it might come from a lost epic). Nestor's speeches regularly use the past as a model for the present; the story of Ereuthalion that follows is the classic example.

title: Nestor's duel with Ereuthalion (Celadon, Pheia, Iardanus)
greek: ὠκυρόῳ Κελάδοντι ... Φειᾶς πὰρ τείχεσσιν, Ἰαρδάνου ἀμφὶ ῥέεθρα (ōkyroōi Keladonti ... Pheias par teichessin, Iardanou amphi rheethra)
short: Nestor's youthful single combat with the giant Ereuthalion is told as a model for the duel Hector proposes; its geography puzzled ancient and modern scholars.
body: Nestor tells how, though the youngest of all, he alone accepted Ereuthalion's challenge, and killed 'the tallest and strongest man that ever I slew' (7.150-6; the story is touched on at 4.319). The tale is a paradeigma, an example from the past that shames the present, and it works: nine heroes stand up. The setting is a puzzle. Leaf identifies Pheia with the Pheia of Od. 15.297 in Elis, a coastal town not near Arcadia, and notes that no river Celadon or Iardanus is known there. Strabo records attempts to emend the names, and Pausanias (5.5.9) reports an Ephesian's claim that the Arcadian Acidas was anciently called the Iardanus, though he found no evidence for it. Leaf observes that keladōn, 'roaring', looks like an adjective, and that 'Iardanus' recalls the Semitic name Jordan (a Cretan river at Od. 3.292). Some guides at Olympia read a scene on the Chest of Cypselus as Pylians and Arcadians about to fight by Pheia and the Iardanus, a reading Pausanias himself rejects (Paus. 5.18.6).

anchor: there stood up nine in all
title: The nine volunteers
greek: οἱ δ᾽ ἐννέα πάντες ἀνέσταν (hoi d' ennea pantes anestan)
short: Shamed by Nestor, nine Greek leaders volunteer; the little catalogue ranks the chieftains and reappears, with Teucer as ninth, in Book 8.
body: Agamemnon springs up first, then Diomedes, the two Aiantes, Idomeneus and his comrade Meriones, Eurypylus, Thoas and finally Odysseus. The order is roughly one of rank and martial prestige, with the king of men at its head. Menelaus, already restrained, and Akhilleus, absent, are missing. The run of lines from the Aiantes to Eurypylus (7.164-7) returns almost unchanged at 8.262-5, where Teucer arrives 'as the ninth' to stand under Ajax's shield; Leaf, commenting on that passage, notes that of the heroes repeated from Book 7 only the greater Ajax actually does anything there. The count of nine thus links the two books. Nestor then proposes the lot, so that no volunteer need be preferred over the others.

title: Choosing a champion by lot
greek: κλῆρον ἐσημήναντο ἕκαστος, ἐν δ᾽ ἔβαλον κυνέῃ (klēron esēmēnanto hekastos, en d' ebalon kyneēi)
short: The volunteers mark their lots and shake them in a helmet; the one that leaps out names the champion, leaving the choice to the gods.
body: Each man put a personal mark (sēma) on his lot, and the lots were shaken in Agamemnon's helmet until one 'leapt out' (LSJ s.v. klēros cites this passage). The herald carried it round the circle endexia, 'from left to right', the lucky direction (LSJ; Leaf), and no one recognised it until it came to Ajax, who knew his mark at a glance. Leaf points out that the mark cannot have been writing, since only its owner understood it. The army's prayer that the lot fall on Ajax, Diomedes or Agamemnon (7.179-80) shows that sortition was understood as letting Zeus choose. Lots had already decided who should cast first in the duel of Paris and Menelaus (3.314-25); Leaf notes that Ajax waives that privilege when he tells Hector to begin (7.232), a mark of confident superiority.

title: 'Mycene rich in gold'
greek: πολυχρύσοιο Μυκήνης (polychrysoio Mykēnēs)
short: Agamemnon's city is 'rich in gold', an epithet strikingly confirmed when Schliemann found the gold-filled Shaft Graves at Mycenae in 1876.
body: polychrysos, 'rich in gold', is used of Mycenae here and at 11.46 (LSJ), and Sophocles echoes it at the opening of the Electra (line 9). Murray keeps Homer's singular form 'Mycene' beside the more usual plural Mycenae. In 1876 Heinrich Schliemann excavated Grave Circle A at Mycenae and found gold masks, cups and jewellery from the sixteenth century BC, many centuries before any date proposed for the Iliad. The epithet is therefore usually taken as a memory of Mycenae's Bronze Age wealth preserved in traditional formulaic diction, though how directly the epic remembers that world remains debated. Leaf, writing after the excavations, often draws on the Mycenae finds, for example on burial practice (note on 7.85) and on the tower-shield (note on 7.219).

title: Ajax's silent prayer, and Salamis
greek: σιγῇ ἐφ᾽ ὑμείων, ἵνα μὴ Τρῶές γε πύθωνται (sigēi eph' hymeiōn, hina mē Trōes ge pythōntai)
short: Ajax asks the army to pray silently so the Trojans cannot hear, then corrects himself: let them pray aloud, he fears no one. He names his home, Salamis.
body: Leaf explains the first request by a widespread belief that a god could be won over by a particular form of words, which had to be hidden from enemies who might counter it with prayers of their own; he compares the secret name of Rome's protecting god and the Jewish avoidance of pronouncing the divine name. Ajax's quick self-correction ('nay, or openly, if ye will') shows his blunt confidence. Zenodotus, Aristophanes and Aristarchus athetized 7.195-9 as out of character and self-contradictory; Leaf finds it natural that a hero should recommend a conventional precaution and then scorn it. Ajax's claim that he was 'born and reared in Salamis' is, apart from the disputed 2.557-8, the only Homeric link between Ajax and the island; Pindar alludes to it (Nemean 2.13-14), and Leaf suspects the couplet may support a later local tradition.

title: Ajax advances like Ares, smiling
greek: μειδιόων βλοσυροῖσι προσώπασι (meidiōn blosyroisi prosōpasi)
short: Ajax strides out like Ares himself, 'smiling with grim face': one of the Iliad's most memorable images of a warrior's joy in battle.
body: He goes 'as huge Ares goeth forth' to war (7.208-10), a comparison Leaf sets beside 13.298-303, where Ares and his son Terror go out to battle. The adjective blosyros probably first meant 'shaggy, bristling' (LSJ, and Adam as cited by Leaf), sinking later into 'grim, fearful'; Plato even uses it of a manly, 'burly' character (Republic 535b). The paradox of a smile on a fearsome face conveys exhilaration rather than cruelty, and its effect on both armies is immediate: the Argives rejoice, trembling seizes the Trojans, and Hector's own heart beats fast (7.214-16). Ajax's title 'bulwark of the Achaeans' (herkos Achaiōn, 7.211) sums up his defensive role, which his great shield makes visible.

title: Ajax's tower-shield
greek: σάκος ἠύτε πύργον, χάλκεον, ἑπταβόειον (sakos ēute pyrgon, chalkeon, heptaboeion)
short: Ajax's huge body-shield, 'like a tower', made by Tychius of seven ox-hides faced with bronze: his emblem throughout Greek tradition.
body: Murray's 'like a city wall' renders ēute pyrgon, literally 'like a tower'. Leaf links the description with the tall oblong body-shields of Mycenaean art and notes that the shield became Ajax's constant attribute: it was the favourite type on the coins of Salamis, and his son was named Eurysakes, 'Broad-shield'. The maker Tychius (a name Leaf sees as a pun on teuchōn, 'making') lived at Hyle in Boeotia and was 'far best of workers in hide'. The shield had seven layers of bull's hide, dried and sewn together, with an eighth layer of bronze nailed on top (heptaboeios, LSJ). The duel tests it exactly: Hector's spear pierces the bronze and six hides and stops in the seventh (7.245-8). Hector's boast that he can swing his shield 'to right and to left' (7.238) describes, according to Reichel as cited by Leaf, the two movements possible with such a shield: slung round the back for retreat, or brought forward to cover the breast.

anchor: tread the measure of furious Ares
title: 'Dancing to Ares'
greek: οἶδα δ᾽ ἐνὶ σταδίῃ δηΐῳ μέλπεσθαι Ἄρηϊ (oida d' eni stadiēi dēiōi melpesthai Arēi)
short: Hector boasts that he knows how to 'dance to Ares' in close combat, imagining battle as a war-dance.
body: melpesthai means to sing and dance in a choral performance. Leaf sees an allusion to war-dances in which warriors mimed a whole battle, a custom that survived into historical Greece as the pyrrhichē; Hector means that he can perform the dance not in play at a feast of Ares but in grim earnest on the battlefield. Aeneas similarly mocks the nimble Meriones as a 'dancer' (orchēstēs) when he dodges a spear (16.617). Hector's reply to Ajax is a catalogue of competences: handling the shield, charging among chariots, and fighting on foot (en stadiēi). He also refuses to strike by stealth, 'spying' for an opening, and will throw 'openly'; Leaf notes that he breaks off so as not to seem to be playing for time.

title: Heralds stop the duel
greek: μέσσῳ δ᾽ ἀμφοτέρων σκῆπτρα σχέθον (messōi d' amphoterōn skēptra schethon)
short: The heralds Talthybius and Idaeus end the fight by holding their staffs between the two heroes: heralds were sacrosanct servants of Zeus.
body: Heralds (kērykes), 'messengers of Zeus and men' (7.274, as at 1.334), were protected by Zeus and could pass between hostile armies. The skēptron, a staff carried by kings, heralds and speakers, here marks an inviolable boundary between the combatants. Leaf points out the chiastic order of 7.275-6 (Trojans, Achaeans; Talthybius, Idaeus). Idaeus appeals to the approach of night: 'it is well to yield obedience to night's behest', which, Leaf says, half personifies Night as a great power controlling men. Ajax insists that Hector, as challenger, should speak first, and Hector's courteous proposal to stop follows. Leaf remarks that such chivalrous acknowledgement of an enemy's prowess is rare in Homer and recalls rather the stories of medieval knighthood.

title: The exchange of gifts: sword and belt
greek: δῶκε ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον ... Αἴας δὲ ζωστῆρα δίδου φοίνικι φαεινόν (dōke xiphos argyroēlon ... Aias de zōstēra didou phoiniki phaeinon)
short: Hector and Ajax part as friends, exchanging a sword and a belt; later legend made both gifts fatal to the men who received them.
body: An exchange of gifts sealed friendship between noble enemies, as when Glaucus and Diomedes swap armour in Book 6 (6.230-6). Hector proposes the gifts so that both peoples may say the two men 'fought in rivalry of soul-devouring strife, but parted in friendship' (7.301-2). He gives his silver-studded sword with its scabbard and baldric; Ajax gives his belt bright with crimson. Leaf notes that later legend turned both gifts into instruments of death. In Sophocles' Ajax the hero falls on Hector's sword, reflecting that 'the gifts of enemies are no gifts' (661-5), and Teucer imagines Hector lashed to Akhilleus' chariot rail by the belt Ajax gave him (1028-33). In the Iliad itself Akhilleus drags Hector by ox-hide thongs passed through his ankles (22.396-8), so the belt detail is post-Homeric.

title: The portion of honour
greek: νώτοισιν δ᾽ Αἴαντα διηνεκέεσσι γέραιρεν (nōtoisin d' Aianta diēnekeessi gerairen)
short: At the victory feast Agamemnon honours Ajax with the whole length of the chine, the prized cut of meat that marks a hero's status.
body: The 'equal feast' (dais eisē, 7.320) gave every man his share, but the best portion publicly marked rank. The verb gerairen comes from geras, the 'gift of honour' or prerogative (LSJ), the material token of honour (timē) whose loss starts the quarrel of Book 1. Leaf compares Herodotus' report that Spartan kings received the backs of all sacrificial victims (6.56) and Virgil's Aeneas feasting on 'the long chine of an ox' (Aen. 8.183); the chine is the honour portion also at 9.207 and in the Odyssey (4.65, 8.475, 14.437). Leaf adds that the sacrifice is told almost entirely in stock lines (compare 1.465-8 and 2.402-3), a reminder that feasts, like arming and battle, are typical scenes in oral composition.

title: Bringing the bones home
greek: ὥς κ᾽ ὀστέα παισὶν ἕκαστος οἴκαδ᾽ ἄγῃ (hōs k' ostea paisin hekastos oikad' agēi)
short: Nestor proposes burning the dead so that each man may carry bones home; Aristarchus rejected the lines because a common mound contradicts it.
body: Cremation is the normal Homeric rite. The idea of repatriating ashes is familiar from classical Athens: in Aeschylus' Agamemnon (435-44) the war-god sends home from Troy urns of ash in place of men. In Homer, however, Leaf finds the practice nowhere else. Aristarchus athetized 7.334-5 on the ground that a single common tomb for all (7.336) is inconsistent with each man carrying bones home; Leaf agrees and calls 7.334 'ludicrously feeble' in expression, since it ought to mean 'that every man may carry his own bones back'. In modern scholarship Denys Page (History and the Homeric Iliad, 1959, pp. 315-24) went further and argued that the wall-building passage of Book 7 is a later Athenian insertion; others defend it. The debate is tied to the larger problem of the Achaean wall.

title: The Achaean wall
greek: πύργους ὑψηλούς, εἶλαρ νηῶν τε καὶ αὐτῶν (pyrgous hypsēlous, eilar nēōn te kai autōn)
short: The Greeks fortify their camp with a wall, gates and a staked ditch: crucial for the battles of Books 8-15, and one of the most debated passages in Homeric criticism.
body: Nestor's plan (7.336-43) is carried out in almost the same words (7.433-41). 'Lofty wall' renders pyrgous hypsēlous, 'high ramparts' (Leaf: pyrgoi here means ramparts, not towers). Why build it only in the tenth year? Thucydides (1.11) assumed the camp was fortified on landing. Leaf thought two versions of the story had been fused, one with an open camp and one with a wall, and called this passage a 'perfunctory and shame-faced makeshift' preparing for the assault on the camp in Book 8. Aristotle, quoted by Strabo (13.1.36), cut the knot: 'the poet who made it up made it vanish', referring to its obliteration by Poseidon and Apollo foretold at 7.459-63 and narrated at 12.3-35. M. L. West defended its narrative purpose (Classical Review 1969), and Ruth Scodel read its destruction as part of a myth of the end of the heroic age (HSCP 86, 1982, 33-50).

title: Antenor's proposal to return Helen
greek: δεῦτ᾽ ἄγετ᾽, Ἀργείην Ἑλένην καὶ κτήμαθ᾽ ἅμ᾽ αὐτῇ δώομεν (deut' aget', Argeiēn Helenēn kai ktēmath' ham' autēi dōomen)
short: In a stormy Trojan assembly Antenor proposes giving back Helen and her treasure; Paris refuses Helen but offers the goods, and Priam proposes a truce to bury the dead.
body: Antenor, who had once hosted Menelaus and Odysseus as envoys (3.205-24), argues that fighting on after breaking the oaths can bring no profit. Paris replies curtly: he will return the treasure he brought from Argos and add more of his own, but not his wife. Leaf, following Erhardt, thought this assembly originally followed the broken truce of Books 3-4, since it presupposes the breach (7.351, 7.402, 7.411). In its present place it shows a city divided: when Idaeus reports the offer he adds, unasked, 'though verily the Trojans bid him do it' (7.393), and Leaf sees Antenor as the spokesman of a popular party. Priam does not overrule his son; he proposes only a truce for burning the dead. Diomedes' reply the next morning makes the offer irrelevant: the 'cords of destruction' are already fastened on Troy.

title: 'Priam, son of Dardanus'
greek: Δαρδανίδης Πρίαμος, θεόφιν μήστωρ ἀτάλαντος (Dardanidēs Priamos, theophin mēstōr atalantos)
short: 'Son of Dardanus' means descendant: Dardanus, son of Zeus, founded the royal line five generations before Priam.
body: Greek patronymics in -idēs can refer to any ancestor, not only the father. Aeneas recites the family tree at 20.215-40: Zeus fathered Dardanus, who founded Dardania on the slopes of Ida before Ilios existed; then came Erichthonius, Tros, Ilus, Laomedon and Priam, while Aeneas descends from Tros' other son Assaracus. Hence the Trojans and their kin are often called 'Dardanians' (Dardanoi), and Leaf notes the rare patronymic form Dardaniōnes, used only at 7.414 and 8.154, formed like 'sons of the Achaeans'. Priam's epithet 'peer of the gods in counsel' (theophin mēstōr atalantos) matches Helenus' address to Hector, 'peer of Zeus in counsel' (7.47): the royal house is marked by wisdom in speech, though it cannot save the city.

title: 'The cords of destruction'
greek: ὀλέθρου πείρατ᾽ ἐφῆπται (olethrou peirat' ephēptai)
short: Diomedes says the 'ends' or 'ropes' of destruction are already fastened on the Trojans; scholars debate whether peirata means 'issues' or 'cords'.
body: Murray translates concretely: the 'cords' of destruction are 'made fast' upon Troy. The noun peirar can mean a rope or knot (Od. 12.51, 162) and also, abstractly, an end or limit; Menelaus' line at 7.102, where Murray has 'the issues of victory are holden of the immortal gods', uses the same word. Leaf surveys the debate at length: either one word whose abstract sense ('end') developed a technical meaning ('rope's end'), or two separate words. He concludes that the abstract sense, 'issues, consummation', is usually preferable, though here the verb ephēptai, 'is fastened upon', suggests the rope, and the gods are elsewhere pictured pulling tight the rope of strife over the armies (13.358-60). Either way the line is a prophecy: Troy's doom is already sealed, and the army shouts its approval.

title: Oath on the sceptre; the burial truce
greek: τὸ σκῆπτρον ἀνέσχεθε πᾶσι θεοῖσιν (to skēptron aneschethe pasi theoisin)
short: Agamemnon seals the truce for burning the dead by raising his sceptre to the gods and calling Zeus, 'loud-thundering lord of Hera', to witness.
body: The sceptre serves as the instrument of an oath here as at 1.234-9, where Akhilleus swears by it, and at 10.321-31, where Hector swears to Dolon (Leaf). Agamemnon names only Zeus, the presiding god of oaths; Leaf finds it unclear why he raises the staff to 'all the gods'. He also observes that, if the author of this passage knew of the broken truce of Book 4, some allusion to it would seem 'imperative' at this point. The truce itself rests on a code both sides share: Agamemnon declares that no one should grudge dead men 'the speedy consolation of fire' (7.409-10). Leaf explains the phrase as 'no grudging concerning the dead, as to giving them the solace of fire quickly'. Burial truces of this kind remained a recognised convention of Greek warfare.

anchor: suffer his folk to wail aloud
title: Gathering the dead in silence
greek: οὐδ᾽ εἴα κλαίειν Πρίαμος μέγας (oud' eia klaiein Priamos megas)
short: During the truce both sides gather and burn their dead; Priam forbids the Trojans to wail aloud, and they mourn in silence.
body: The scene is among the most humane in the poem: the bodies are hard to recognise until the blood is washed off, and the men load the wagons 'shedding hot tears'. Priam forbids loud lament, so the Trojans mourn in silence, and the Achaeans do the same on their side (7.431-2); the contrast with the formal laments at Hector's funeral (24.719-76) is striking. Leaf notes the confused chronology of this part of the book: Idaeus seems to return with the Greek answer before sunrise (7.381, 7.421), and the passing of the night is not clearly marked, which is unlike normal epic style. The dawn lines 7.421-2 recur at Od. 19.433-4, and Leaf thinks the Odyssey borrowed them from here.

title: Poseidon's complaint and the walls of Troy
greek: ὅ τ᾽ ἐγὼ καὶ Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων ἥρῳ Λαομέδοντι πολίσσαμεν ἀθλήσαντε (ho t' egō kai Phoibos Apollōn hērōi Laomedonti polissamen athlēsante)
short: Poseidon, the 'Shaker of Earth', fears the Greek wall will outshine the walls of Troy that he and Apollo built for Laomedon; Zeus lets him destroy it later.
body: Poseidon's titles enosichthōn and ennosigaios, 'Earth-shaker', mark him as god of earthquakes as well as the sea. He complains that the Achaeans built without offering hecatombs and that their wall's fame will eclipse his own work. Troy's walls were built by Poseidon and Apollo for King Laomedon, who then refused their wages; Poseidon recalls this bitterly at 21.441-57, and Apollodorus (2.5.9) adds that Apollo sent a plague and Poseidon a sea-monster in revenge. Hence the Trojans' 'battlement builded of the gods' (theodmētos, 8.519). Zeus answers that once the Greeks sail home Poseidon may sweep the wall into the sea, as told at 12.3-35. Zenodotus, Aristophanes and Aristarchus rejected 7.443-64 because Book 12 retells the destruction with no reference to this scene; Leaf sees two parallel versions, 'both late'.

title: Euneus of Lemnos and the Argonauts
greek: Ἰησονίδης Εὔνηος, τόν ῥ᾽ ἔτεχ᾽ Ὑψιπύλη ὑπ᾽ Ἰήσονι (Iēsonidēs Eunēos, ton rh' etech' Hypsipylē hyp' Iēsoni)
short: Wine arrives from Lemnos, sent by Euneus, son of the Argonaut Jason and the Lemnian queen Hypsipyle: one of Homer's few glances at the Argonaut legend.
body: When the Argonauts put in at Lemnos, whose women had killed their menfolk, the queen Hypsipyle slept with Jason and bore him sons, Euneus and Nebrophonus (Apollodorus 1.9.17). Leaf lists the other Homeric allusions to the Argonauts: Euneus buys Akhilleus' captive Lycaon (21.40-1) and pays for him with a silver mixing-bowl (23.740-7), and the Odyssey calls the Argo 'known to all' (Od. 12.69-72). Lemnos here appears as a friendly neutral trading post supplying the camp, though at 9.72 the Greeks' wine comes from Thrace. Euneus' private gift of 'a thousand measures' (metra, a recognised quantity, Leaf) to the sons of Atreus is a courtesy to the commanders. Agamemnon will later recall the Greeks' drunken boasts on Lemnos (8.229-34).

title: Barter in the Greek camp
greek: ἄλλοι μὲν χαλκῷ, ἄλλοι δ᾽ αἴθωνι σιδήρῳ, ἄλλοι δὲ ῥινοῖς ... ἄλλοι δ᾽ ἀνδραπόδεσσι (alloi men chalkōi, alloi d' aithōni sidērōi, alloi de rhinois ... alloi d' andrapodessi)
short: The Greeks buy wine by barter, paying in bronze, iron, hides, live cattle and slaves: a snapshot of an economy without coinage.
body: There is no coined money in Homer. Values are reckoned in oxen, as in the famous exchange of gold armour 'worth a hundred oxen' for bronze 'worth nine' (6.235-6), and trade is conducted in goods. Iron, called 'gleaming' (aithōn), is a valuable commodity, as the iron lump offered as a prize at 23.826-35 shows. Leaf explains autēisi boessin as whole, live oxen as opposed to hides. The last item, 'slaves' (andrapodessi), was athetized by Zenodotus, Aristophanes and Aristarchus because the word andrapodon was thought unknown to Homer; Leaf adds that this dative form occurs nowhere else in Greek. The verb oinizonto, 'they got themselves wine', recurs when the Trojans fetch wine at 8.506 (Leaf). The scene shows the besieging camp supplied by sea like a market town.

title: Night of evil omen; libation; the gift of sleep
greek: οἶνον δ᾽ ἐκ δεπάων χαμάδις χέον (oinon d' ek depaōn chamadis cheon)
short: Zeus thunders all night as an evil omen; in fear the men pour wine on the ground to him before drinking, then take 'the gift of sleep'.
body: A libation was poured to the gods before drinking; here terror makes it urgent, and 'no man durst drink until he had made a drink-offering to the son of Cronos'. Leaf insists the warning thunder is meant for both sides alike, foreshadowing the coming battles; 'Zeus the counsellor devised them evil' leads straight into Book 8, where his thunder dominates the fighting. The book ends with 'the gift of sleep' (hypnou dōron), a formula that recurs at 9.713, Od. 16.481 and 19.427 and means the gift that consists in sleep. Zenodotus omitted 7.482 and placed the first line of Book 8 after 8.52, so that the divine council happens a day earlier and connects more closely with these omens (Leaf on 8.1).
